title: Plan a release
summary: A release plan makes sure everyone knows what is going out, when, who is affected and what happens if it goes wrong. Releasing small changes gradually keeps the risk low.

beginner: Write one page that says what is in the release, who it affects, the goal and what is not included.
List everyone who needs to know: support teams, stakeholders, other teams who depend on you, and users if their experience changes. Plan what each group will hear and when.
Agree with your engineers how the change goes live. Releasing to a small share of users first (sometimes called a canary or phased release) lets you spot problems before everyone sees them.
Agree how you will know it is working: the dashboards and alerts to watch, and who watches them in the first hours and days.
Agree a rollback plan: what would make you undo the release, who decides and how long it takes.
Check the go-live list with the team the day before: tests passed, support briefed, monitoring ready, comms scheduled. After release, check your measures and share how it went.
intermediate: Publish a release page covering scope, goal, audience, non-goals and timeline.
Plan stakeholder, support and user communications.
Agree a gradual rollout, monitoring, owners and rollback criteria with engineering.
Run a go / no-go check and a short review after release.
experienced: Publish the scope, audience and comms plan.
Plan a gradual rollout with monitoring and named owners.
Agree the rollback criteria and who makes the decision.
Hold a go / no-go meeting, and book a post-release review.

canDelegateTo.task: Coordinate the release timeline, go / no-go meeting and dependencies
Set up the gradual rollout, monitoring, alerts and rollback
Write user-facing release notes and messages
Confirm testing is complete and run smoke tests after release

toolExamples.jira: Create a version (release) and attach the stories to it, so the release notes and progress come from one place.
toolExamples.confluence: Use a release planning page: background, goals and non-goals, team, timeline, comms and rollback plan.
toolExamples.github: Ask engineers to tag the release, so you can see exactly what went out and roll back to the previous tag if needed.
toolExamples.vercel: Every pull request gets a preview link for checking before it goes live, and you can promote an earlier deployment back to production if something breaks.
toolExamples.aws: Ask DevOps whether the service can shift traffic gradually to the new version, so problems only reach a small share of users.
toolExamples.azure: Ask DevOps about deployment slots, which let you test a release in production conditions and swap back quickly.

definitionOfDone: Release scope, audience and timeline published
Stakeholders, support and users told what they need to know
Monitoring and named owners in place for the first days
pitfalls: Releasing everything to everyone at once
Support teams hearing about changes from users
No agreed point at which you would undo the release

sources.title: A product manager's guide to release planning (Atlassian)
